title: Looking back: on nostalgia
context_es: Una revista internacional de arte y cultura invita a sus lectores a escribir para una serie titulada «Looking back».
prompt_en: An international arts and culture magazine has invited readers to contribute to a series entitled 'Looking back'. Write an article in which you describe something from the past that you feel nostalgic about, consider why nostalgia has such a powerful hold on people, and assess whether it does us more good than harm.
points: describe something you feel nostalgic about
consider why nostalgia has such a hold on people
assess whether it does more good than harm
useful_language: I have come to suspect that …
What I miss is not … but …
And yet I would not be without it.
Looked at squarely, … is neither … nor …
tips_es: Un artículo de C2 se sostiene en la voz: una imagen concreta para abrir, una idea que avanza y un cierre que resuena.
Varía el ritmo: frases largas y trabajadas junto a alguna muy corta (*They were not, of course.*).
Hay tres cosas que hacer (describir, explicar, valorar): que no se quede ninguna sin su párrafo.
model_answer:
The summer that never ended

There is a photograph on my desk of a village square in August: plastic chairs, a string of coloured bulbs and, in the corner, a boy of nine holding an ice cream that is about to fall. I am that boy, and for years I have been convinced that the summers of my childhood were longer, hotter and happier than any I have known since.

They were not, of course. The diaries my mother kept record storms, mosquito bites and endless complaints of boredom. What I miss is not the place itself, which I could visit tomorrow, but a version of myself for whom time was not yet in short supply. Nostalgia, I have come to suspect, is rarely about the past at all. It is the present, wearing a disguise, telling us what it lacks.

That would explain why the feeling grows stronger in periods of upheaval. When the future looks uncertain, memory offers a country whose borders are fixed and whose ending we already know. Small wonder that advertisers and politicians alike have learnt to trade on it, selling us reissued trainers and promises to bring back an age that never quite existed.

Herein lies the danger. A nostalgia that edits out the storms can curdle into resentment of the present and suspicion of anything new. Entire communities have been persuaded that their best days are behind them, which is a poor foundation on which to build anything.

And yet I would not be without it. Psychologists have found that recalling cherished moments makes people feel less lonely and more generous, and I can well believe it. That photograph does not make me want to be nine again; it reminds me to telephone my sister, who is just out of shot, laughing.

Looked at squarely, then, nostalgia is neither a sickness nor a refuge. It is a letter from our younger selves, and the wisest course is to read it with affection, and then to write back.
